cards.heading: Why reach for C++ at all
cards.hook: A pure JavaScript image processing routine took 45 seconds — the same operation as a native C++ addon took 0.8 seconds, a 56x gain.
cards.body: Bcrypt-style hashing was 18x faster, and parsing a 100MB CSV was 6.6x faster while using 82% less memory.

cards.heading: When addons are the wrong tool
cards.hook: I/O-bound work, simple CRUD, network requests, and file system operations are already async in Node — a C++ addon adds complexity without adding speed there.
cards.body: Reach for one for CPU-intensive computation: image/video processing, cryptography, scientific simulation, or wrapping an existing native library.

cards.heading: V8 API vs N-API
cards.hook: The raw V8 API gives maximum performance and control but breaks across Node versions, forcing a recompile — N-API trades a little overhead for a stable ABI that survives upgrades.

cards.heading: node-gyp is the build system
cards.hook: node-gyp compiles your C++ source into a platform-specific .node binary, generating the right Makefile or Visual Studio project for whatever OS it's running on.

cards.heading: binding.gyp is the addon's build config
cards.hook: target_name sets the output binary's name, sources lists the C++ files to compile, and cflags! removes a default flag — here, to re-enable C++ exceptions.

cards.heading: NODE_MODULE registers the addon
cards.hook: Every addon ends with a NODE_MODULE macro call that hands Node an Initialize function — that's the one hook point where your C++ functions become visible as a JS exports object.

cards.heading: Every exported function has the same shape
cards.hook: An addon function always takes a FunctionCallbackInfo<Value>& and returns void — you set the actual return value through args.GetReturnValue().Set(...), not a C++ return statement.

cards.heading: An Isolate is one V8 VM instance
cards.hook: Every V8 operation needs an Isolate pointer, and isolates are not thread-safe — a worker thread must get its own isolate, never reuse one from the main thread.

cards.heading: A Context is an execution environment
cards.hook: Most V8 operations — setting an object property, calling a function — require the current Context, not just the Isolate, because it's what separates one global object and execution scope from another.

cards.heading: Local handles clean themselves up
cards.hook: A Local<> handle is stack-allocated and vanishes the moment its scope exits — fine for temporary values, but useless for anything that needs to outlive the function call.

cards.heading: Persistent handles survive garbage collection
cards.hook: A Persistent<> handle is heap-allocated and keeps a V8 value alive across calls — the right choice for a stored callback or any long-lived object — but it must be explicitly Reset() or it leaks.

cards.heading: HandleScope is what makes Local safe in a loop
cards.hook: Without a HandleScope inside a million-iteration loop, a million Local handles would pile up and never get released — a scope created each iteration cleans them up the moment that iteration ends.

cards.heading: Check types before you convert
cards.hook: Calling NumberValue on an argument that's actually a string doesn't throw — it just silently gives you a wrong number, which is why every addon function checks IsNumber/IsString/IsArray before touching args.

cards.heading: Everything starts as a Local<Value>
cards.hook: Every JavaScript value crossing into C++ arrives as the same generic Local<Value> — you only get a Number, String, or Array once you've checked its type and explicitly cast with .As<T>().

cards.heading: JavaScript numbers are all 64-bit floats
cards.hook: There's no separate JS integer type — every number, including what looks like an integer, is IEEE 754 double precision, safe only up to 2^53-1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER).

cards.heading: Four ways to pull a number out of a Value
cards.hook: NumberValue gives you a double, Int32Value/Uint32Value give fixed-width integers, and IntegerValue gives an int64 — pick based on what the C++ side actually needs, not just what compiles.

cards.heading: String::Utf8Value is the quick string bridge
cards.hook: Wrapping a JS value in String::Utf8Value gives you a C string via dereferencing it — it's stack-allocated and cheap, but its lifetime is tied to that scope, so convert to std::string if you need the data afterward.
cards.code:
String::Utf8Value str(isolate, args[0]);
const char* cstr = *str;

cards.heading: A UTF-8 string's length is in bytes, not characters
cards.hook: utf8.length() on a string containing non-ASCII characters (like 世界) counts bytes, not visible characters — getting the real character count needs a proper UTF-8-aware parser.

cards.heading: Truthy and falsy convert exactly like JS
cards.hook: BooleanValue() applies JavaScript's own truthiness rules — false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN all convert to false, and literally everything else converts to true.

cards.heading: Building a V8 array means setting each index
cards.hook: There's no bulk constructor from a C++ vector — Array::New(isolate, length) allocates the slots, then you loop and Set() each one from your std::vector<double> or similar.

cards.heading: Reading an object's properties by name
cards.hook: obj->Get(context, key) fetches a property, obj->Has(context, key) checks existence first without throwing, and GetPropertyNames() enumerates every key on the object — the same three operations you'd reach for in JS.

cards.heading: ArrayBuffer + BackingStore is zero-copy binary data
cards.hook: GetBackingStore() hands you a raw uint8_t* pointer straight into the buffer's actual memory — you can read or modify it in place without ever copying the bytes through a JS-side array.
cards.code:
auto backing = buffer->GetBackingStore();
uint8_t* data = static_cast<uint8_t*>(backing->Data());

cards.heading: A TypedArray is a view, not its own storage
cards.hook: A Uint8Array or Float64Array doesn't own memory — it has a ByteOffset and ByteLength into a shared underlying ArrayBuffer, so two typed array views can read and write the exact same bytes.

cards.heading: Don't convert the same value twice
cards.hook: Wrapping the same argument in String::Utf8Value more than once in the same function silently redoes the UTF-8 decode — convert it once, keep the std::string, and reuse it.

cards.heading: Hoist repeated V8 object creation out of loops
cards.hook: Creating the same Local<String> key inside a thousand-iteration loop rebuilds it a thousand times — create it once outside the loop and reuse the handle on every pass.

cards.heading: Node.js has one thread — don't block it
cards.hook: A synchronous C++ call that takes 5 seconds freezes the entire event loop for those 5 seconds: no HTTP requests handled, no timers fire, the whole app looks hung.
cards.body: The rule of thumb: any operation over roughly 10ms must run asynchronously.

cards.heading: libuv's thread pool defaults to 4 threads
cards.hook: Every async addon operation that needs real CPU work runs on libuv's background thread pool, which is only 4 threads by default — tunable with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable.

cards.heading: uv_queue_work is the core async pattern
cards.hook: You hand libuv two functions: one that runs the expensive work on a background thread, and one that runs back on the main thread once it's done — that's the entire mechanism async addons are built on.
cards.code:
uv_queue_work(uv_default_loop(), &data->request,
  ExecuteWork,    // worker thread
  WorkComplete);  // main thread

cards.heading: Never touch V8 objects from a worker thread
cards.hook: The function libuv runs in the background thread must stay pure C++ — touching any V8/Isolate object there is a guaranteed crash, since V8 objects are only safe on the thread that owns them.

cards.heading: A work struct carries data across the thread boundary
cards.hook: Because the worker and completion functions run on different threads, you can't use normal stack variables — a heap-allocated struct holding the uv_work_t, a Persistent<Function> callback, and your input/output fields is what ties the two halves together.

cards.heading: Modern addons return real Promises
cards.hook: Promise::Resolver::New creates a promise and its resolver up front; the background work resolves or rejects it from the main-thread completion callback once the result is ready — then async/await on the JS side just works.

cards.heading: uv_async_send reports progress mid-flight
cards.hook: A worker thread can call uv_async_send to safely wake a callback on the main thread before the whole job finishes — that's how a long-running addon reports 10%, 20%, 30% progress back to JavaScript.

cards.heading: Cancellation is cooperative, not forced
cards.hook: There's no way to kill a running worker thread outright — cancellation means setting an atomic bool flag and having the worker check it periodically between units of work, bailing out early if it's set.

cards.heading: The completion handler owns cleanup
cards.hook: Whatever heap-allocated work struct you created before queuing the job gets deleted in the completion callback, and any Persistent<Function> you stashed gets Reset() there too — forgetting either one leaks on every single call.

cards.heading: Without wrapping, every call starts from zero
cards.hook: A plain exported function like addon.add(5, 3) can't remember anything between calls — object wrapping is what lets new addon.Calculator(10) keep its running value across calc.add(5) and calc.multiply(2).

cards.heading: node::ObjectWrap ties a C++ instance to a JS object
cards.hook: Inheriting from node::ObjectWrap and calling Wrap(args.This()) in your constructor binds a real C++ object underneath a JavaScript object — Unwrap<T>() in every method call gets it back out.

cards.heading: SetInternalFieldCount(1) is easy to forget
cards.hook: Wrap() needs a slot on the JS object to stash the C++ pointer in — skip SetInternalFieldCount(1) on the instance template and Wrap() has nowhere to put it.

cards.heading: A constructor callback has to handle both call styles
cards.hook: JavaScript can call a constructor function with or without new — args.IsConstructCall() is how the C++ side tells which happened, and the non-new branch just forwards to a real construct call manually.

cards.heading: Properties feel more native than method calls
cards.hook: SetAccessor on the instance template wires up a getter and setter pair, so calc.value reads naturally instead of requiring calc.getValue() — a small touch that makes a wrapped class feel like a real JS object.

cards.heading: The destructor fires on garbage collection
cards.hook: A wrapped object's C++ destructor runs automatically once the JS object it's bound to gets garbage collected — the natural place to close a file handle or release any other resource it's holding.

cards.heading: Wrapped objects can be passed between functions
cards.hook: Unwrap() doesn't only work inside a class's own methods — any function can unwrap an object passed in as an argument, which is how one addon function hands a C++ instance off to another.

cards.heading: A factory function skips the new keyword
cards.hook: A plain exported function can internally call the stored constructor and hand back a fully wrapped instance — addon.createObject(42) instead of new addon.MyObject(42), useful when you want a function-style API.

cards.heading: When object wrapping actually earns its complexity
cards.hook: Stateful operations, system resources like files or database connections, and complex data structures like trees or graphs are where wrapping pays off — a one-shot stateless calculation doesn't need it.

cards.heading: A flat addon directory stops scaling fast
cards.hook: Dumping every .cc file into the project root works for a weekend prototype, but it breaks down past 2-3 files — no separation between C++ source, JS wrapper, build config, and tests.

cards.heading: Three structure levels, picked by project size
cards.hook: A single small addon just needs src/, test/, and a binding.gyp. Several related addons sharing code graduate to a packages/ monorepo with a common/ folder. A production library adds include/, benchmarks, and TypeScript types.

cards.heading: Shared C++ code lives in its own folder, referenced by path
cards.hook: When multiple addons in a monorepo need the same buffer or string helpers, a common/include + common/src pair gets referenced from each addon's binding.gyp with a relative path, rather than duplicated per addon.

cards.heading: A thin JS wrapper layer hides the native API
cards.hook: Instead of exposing the raw C++ addon directly, a src/js/index.js class wraps it in a clean Promise-based API — consumers never see the callback-style native methods underneath.

cards.heading: Cross-platform code branches on compile-time macros
cards.hook: _WIN32, __APPLE__, and __linux__ are the standard preprocessor checks for platform-specific implementations — a memory allocator might use VirtualAlloc on Windows and mmap everywhere else behind the same function signature.

cards.heading: Ship TypeScript types alongside the native binary
cards.hook: A types/index.d.ts file gives TypeScript consumers full autocomplete and type-checking on a native addon's API, even though the actual implementation is a compiled .node binary with no types of its own.

cards.heading: Unit tests and integration tests stay in separate folders
cards.hook: test/unit holds C++-level tests of individual components, test/integration holds JS-level tests that exercise the compiled addon end-to-end — mixing the two makes it unclear what failed when something breaks.

cards.heading: binding.gyp conditions branch per operating system
cards.hook: A conditions block lets one binding.gyp link pthread only on Linux, set Xcode-specific flags only on macOS, and apply MSVC exception handling only on Windows — all from a single shared build file.

cards.heading: Check argument count before you check types
cards.hook: args[1] on a function called with only one argument doesn't throw, it returns undefined — args.Length() is the first thing every addon function checks, before it ever inspects a single argument's type.

cards.heading: Promises are the async style to reach for now
cards.hook: The raw uv_queue_work + callback pattern still works, but wrapping it behind a Promise::Resolver means the JavaScript side gets normal .then()/await instead of a Node-style error-first callback.

cards.heading: A benchmark folder proves the addon is actually faster
cards.hook: The entire case for writing a C++ addon rests on a measured speedup — a benchmark/ folder with before/after numbers is what turns "it should be faster" into evidence worth shipping.

cards.heading: npm install can trigger the native build automatically
cards.hook: Setting "install": "node-gyp rebuild" as an npm script means consumers of the package never run node-gyp by hand — a plain npm install silently compiles the native binary for their platform.
